idiom_name: assert() at the seam + throw at the first violated precondition (RAII releases on unwind)
implementation_notes: C++ expresses fail-fast with primitives already in the language. assert() (and static_assert) documents invariants that must hold at a point and aborts when one is breached, while a throw ends the operation immediately and stack unwinding runs every destructor, so RAII releases the resources the attempt held. Throw from the entry of a public function - std::invalid_argument / std::logic_error for caller misuse, a domain-specific type otherwise - rather than repairing invalid state, and keep the only catch-all at the top level. Assertions stay justified for programming errors, never for input validation, and must respect the boundary they cross: throwing out of a noexcept function, a destructor or a thread entry point calls std::terminate.
pitfalls: Throwing across a noexcept boundary, a destructor, a C ABI function or a thread entry point calls std::terminate: fail-fast has to respect the boundary it is thrown across.
assert() is compiled out with NDEBUG, so it cannot be the production guard for input or capacity checks.
A catch (...) that logs and continues at an inner level converts the fail-fast throw into fail-slow behaviour and destroys the stack information that made the failure useful.

variants.name: std::expected value-based propagation (C++23)
variants.idiom_name: std::expected<T,E> returned at the first failure + monadic and_then/or_else
variants.implementation_notes: std::expected<T, E> (C++23) carries the failure back as a value: an operation that cannot be served returns std::unexpected(error) at the first check, and the callers' and_then / or_else chains short-circuit at that point, so no exception has to escape. Choose it where exceptions are unavailable or banned (-fno-exceptions, embedded targets, style guides that require explicit error handling) and where the caller must be forced to look at the error; assert/abort remain the right tool for programmer errors. It replaces the exception-based form for the request path, not for invariant checking.
pitfalls: Calling .value() defeats the point: an ignored expected throws std::bad_expected_access at the access site, moving the failure back to a late, unrelated place.
Mixing the two idioms in one module loses the discipline - half the failures unwind and half travel as values, and callers stop knowing which to expect.
std::expected is C++23-only; on C++17 toolchains the equivalent is std::optional plus a separate error channel, which does not compose monadically.
